title: Charged and rotating black holes
part: IV: Orbits, stars, and black holes
one_line_summary: Moves beyond Schwarzschild to the two other stationary black holes: after using the no-hair idea to argue that mass, charge and spin are all that matter, it quotes the Reissner-Nordstrom metric and reads its two horizons, three regions, avoidable timelike singularity and endless Penrose tower, then quotes the Kerr metric in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates and probes it with test particles and light to reveal the ring singularity, frame dragging, the stationary limit and ergosphere, and finally the Penrose process that mines a spinning hole for energy and angular momentum.
role_in_book: Final chapter of Part IV. Chapters 21-27 built the Schwarzschild toolkit (Killing-vector constants of motion, effective potentials for particles and photons, horizons, closed trapped surfaces, Kruskal and Penrose diagrams) and Chapter 28 used the sign change of the timelike Killing vector's norm to explain Hawking radiation. This chapter re-deploys every one of those tools on the charged and rotating solutions, so it functions as a capstone survey rather than a new-formalism chapter: the metrics are quoted, not derived, and most algebra is pushed into exercises. It also supplies the astrophysically essential message that real holes spin. Part V then leaves black holes and rebuilds geometry rigorously; Killing vectors, electromagnetic stress-energy and curvature computations that would justify these metrics return in Chapters 33, 36 and 42.

learning_objectives: Reader can state the no-hair idea and explain why it means mass, charge and angular momentum fully characterize a stationary black hole seen from outside.
Reader can write the Reissner-Nordstrom line element, recover Schwarzschild as q -> 0, and find the horizon radii r± = M ± (M² - q²)^{1/2}.
Reader can classify the regions I, II, III of a two-horizon black hole by whether surfaces of constant r are timelike or spacelike, and say which regions are static.

Reader can read the maximally extended Reissner-Nordstrom Penrose diagram to explain why its r = 0 singularity is timelike and avoidable and why travel to another asymptotically flat region is one-way.
Reader can explain what makes a metric stationary and axisymmetric and why such a metric generically carries a g_tφ cross term.
Reader can write the Kerr metric in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates, identify Δ and ρ², relate a to J and M, and check the a -> 0 and large-r limits.
Reader can locate the ring singularity (ρ = 0) and the horizons (Δ = 0), and state the extremal bound a ≤ M (J ≤ M²).
Reader can compute the Kerr horizon area A = 8πMr+ from the induced 2-metric on the horizon.
Reader can use the conserved u_t and u_φ together with the inverse t-φ metric block to show that a zero-angular-momentum particle acquires dφ/dt = g^{tφ}/g^{tt} (frame dragging).
Reader can derive the coordinate angular velocities of tangential light rays from the null condition and show that where g_tt = 0 one of them vanishes.
Reader can prove that no stationary observer can exist where g_tt ≥ 0 and derive the stationary limit r0 = M + (M² - a² cos²θ)^{1/2}, sketching the ergosphere between r+ and r0.

Reader can explain the Penrose process: why a spacelike Killing vector in the ergosphere permits negative Killing energy, how that lets the escaping fragment carry out more energy than came in, and why the captured fragment must have negative angular momentum.
Reader can interpret the prograde/retrograde asymmetry in the Kerr equatorial effective potentials for particles and photons.

teaching_approach.summary: A brisk survey that treats both new metrics as given and learns about them by interrogation rather than derivation. The authors justify the scope with the no-hair slogan, use the charged hole (admitted to be astrophysically implausible) as a gentler rehearsal of the two-horizon causal structure, and then spend most of the chapter on Kerr. The Kerr geometry is explored in the book's familiar Part IV style: find the Killing vectors, write the conserved quantities, drop in test particles and light rays, and read physics off effective potentials and null conditions. Penrose diagrams and cartoons carry the global structure; formal Example boxes carry the short calculations; the heavier algebra (inverse metric, effective potentials, horizon area) is delegated to exercises. The chapter ends with an application, the Penrose process, deliberately built on the same spacelike-Killing-vector argument used for Hawking radiation in the previous chapter, and with a humble margin essay on how hard the Kerr solution is to derive.
narrative_arc: Motivating claim: Schwarzschild is only the simplest member of a family; the no-hair slogan says external observers can only ever learn M, q and J, so studying charge and spin covers every stationary hole.
Charge first, with a caveat: real holes would neutralize, but allowing q reveals rich structure. Quote the Reissner-Nordstrom metric and check q -> 0.
Find the horizons from the zeros of the metric function; divide spacetime into regions I, II, III and say which are static.
Read the causal story off the infinite Penrose tower: region II traps, region III has a timelike repulsive singularity, and a traveller can pass one-way into a fresh asymptotic region.
Ask what observers would see: infinite redshift at r+ for distant watchers, and a blueshifted fast-forward of region I for someone crossing r-.
Pivot to rotation as the realistic case; Example 29.1 shows the general stationary axisymmetric form and flags the dφ dt cross term as the source of new physics.
Introduce Boyer-Lindquist coordinates, quote the Kerr metric, and run sanity checks (t, φ reversal symmetry, flat at large r, Schwarzschild at a = 0).
Catalogue singular surfaces: ρ = 0 is a physical ring, Δ = 0 gives two horizons, and a ≤ M caps the spin; compute the horizon area (Example 29.2).
Show the Kerr Penrose diagram with its negative-r extension, closed timelike curves and wormhole passages.

Probe the geometry with test bodies: a particle dropped with zero angular momentum still circulates (frame dragging, Example 29.3); equatorial orbits obey a spin-modified effective potential (Example 29.4).

Probe with light: tangential photons satisfy a quadratic null condition (Example 29.5); where g_tt vanishes, counter-rotating light stalls, so no observer can hover, which defines the stationary limit and the ergosphere.
Complete the light picture with the photon effective potential depending on the sense of orbit (Example 29.6) and a light-cone map of the regions.

Application: the Penrose process. Local momentum conservation plus a spacelike Killing vector inside the ergosphere allows a negative-energy fragment to fall in, so energy is extracted; Example 29.7 shows this also spins the hole down.
Close with a summary and a margin essay on the notorious difficulty of deriving and perturbing the Kerr solution.
signature_moves: Scope justified by a theorem slogan: the no-hair metaphor licenses a three-parameter survey instead of an open-ended one.
Rehearsal on a toy: the unrealistic charged hole is used to teach the two-horizon, three-region causal layout that Kerr then repeats.
Global structure read from Penrose diagrams (with lines of constant r and t drawn in) instead of from integrated geodesics.
The Part IV recipe applied to a non-diagonal metric: Killing vectors -> conserved u_t, u_φ -> invert the t-φ block -> read off coordinate velocities.
Photons as the universal speed limit: if the null condition forbids counter-rotating light, it forbids every massive body, so a property of light rays defines a region of spacetime.
One-line impossibility proof: a stationary 4-velocity would need g_tt (u^t)² = -1, which fails once g_tt ≥ 0.
Explicit reuse of the previous chapter's geometric trick (sign flip of ξ·ξ) to power a new phenomenon, the Penrose process, with a footnote that plants the fact early.
Energy bounds obtained by dotting local conservation laws with Killing vectors and with an observer's 4-velocity built from Killing vectors.
Heavy algebra quoted in footnotes and pushed to exercises, keeping the main text a narrative of physical consequences.
Candid admission (margin essay) that the metric is being quoted because its derivation is famously arduous.

sections.title: Chapter opening: more general black holes and no hair
sections.summary: Frames Schwarzschild as the simplest case and announces the two generalizations, charge and rotation, assuming collapse has exposed the central region. Because an event horizon hides the interior, outside observers can only access mass, charge and angular momentum; the no-hair slogan and theorem say these fix the exterior geometry independent of how the hole formed, so the analysis applies broadly.
key_moves: Horizon hides everything except globally measurable charges (M, q, J).
Independence from formation history turns a special-case study into a general one.
Margin notes credit Bekenstein with the phrase and Hawking, Carter and Israel with the theorem.

sections.title: Charged black holes
sections.summary: Concedes that charged holes would neutralize in astrophysical settings, then studies them anyway. The Reissner-Nordstrom line element adds a q²/r² term reflecting electromagnetic field energy; it reduces to Schwarzschild as q -> 0. For q² > M² only r = 0 is singular; for q² ≤ M² two coordinate singularities r± split spacetime into static region I, non-static region II (full of closed trapped surfaces) and static region III, which contains a timelike, repulsive physical singularity. The maximally extended Penrose diagram is an infinite vertical tower of region-I pairs linked through II and III, so a timelike traveller can dodge the singularity and emerge, irreversibly, in a new asymptotically flat universe. Distant observers see infallers infinitely redshifted at r+, while an observer entering region III could see all of a region I's history, strongly blueshifted.
concepts: regions I, II and III of a two-horizon black hole
passage to another asymptotically flat region
key_moves: Justify the q²/r² term as the gravitational effect of electromagnetic energy density on the right-hand side of the field equation.
Solve 1 - 2M/r + q²/r² = 0 to get r± and note three cases: q² > M², q² = M² (no region II), q² < M².
Classify regions by the causal character of constant-r and constant-t surfaces.
Contrast the timelike r = 0 of region III with the spacelike Schwarzschild and Robertson-Walker singularities.
Trace a timelike curve I -> II -> III -> II' -> I' and argue it cannot return.
Discuss what infalling and distant observers see (redshift at r+, blueshifted history near r-).

sections.title: Kerr black holes: metric, coordinates and singular surfaces
sections.summary: Rotation breaks spherical symmetry, so Schwarzschild cannot describe most astrophysical objects; Kerr is introduced as the stationary, axisymmetric, asymptotically flat rotating solution. Example 29.1 gives the general stationary axisymmetric line element with an angular velocity ω producing a dt dφ cross term. Boyer-Lindquist coordinates are defined via a modified spherical-to-Cartesian map, so constant-r surfaces are ellipsoids and r = 0 is not a point. The Kerr metric is quoted with Δ = r² - 2Mr + a² and ρ² = r² + a² cos²θ, component forms, Killing vectors ξ and η, and a rewritten ω-form; a = J/M is the Kerr parameter. Symmetry and limit checks follow. Singular surfaces: ρ = 0 is a physical ring of radius a in the equatorial plane; Δ = 0 gives inner and outer horizons r±, which exist only for a ≤ M, so spin is capped at J = M² (extremal Kerr). Example 29.2 finds the outer horizon area 8πMr+. The Kerr Penrose diagram extends through the ring to negative r; region III contains timelike, avoidable singularities, closed timelike curves and passages to further universes.
concepts: Kerr Penrose diagram with negative r
Killing vectors and conserved quantities in Kerr
key_moves: Argue from stationarity and axisymmetry that components depend only on r and θ and that a cross term is expected.
Map Boyer-Lindquist (r, θ, φ) to Cartesian coordinates to show constant-r surfaces are oblate ellipsoids.
Quote the Kerr metric and verify: invariance under t -> -t with φ -> -φ, Minkowski at large r, Schwarzschild at a = 0.
Separate ρ = 0 (curvature singularity, a ring x² + y² = a², z = 0) from Δ = 0 (coordinate singularities at r±).
Use the square root in r± to derive the extremal bound a ≤ M.
Set dt = dr = 0 at r = r+ and use r+² + a² = 2Mr+ to simplify the horizon 2-metric and integrate its area.
Explain why the Penrose diagram can continue past r = 0 into negative r, unlike Schwarzschild or Reissner-Nordstrom.

sections.title: Kerr black holes: probing with particles and light
sections.summary: Uses test bodies to map the Kerr regions. Conserved u_t = -Ẽ and u_φ = L̃ are written with the cross terms. Example 29.3 raises indices with the inverse t-φ block and shows a particle with u_φ = 0 has dφ/dt = g^{φt}/g^{tt} ≠ 0: inertial frame dragging. Example 29.4 gives equatorial u^t, u^φ in terms of Ẽ, L̃ and a Kerr effective potential with a spin-dependent 1/r² term and a (L̃ - aẼ)² term. Example 29.5 solves the null condition for tangential photons; where g_tt = 0 (ρ² = 2Mr), the co-rotating ray moves at -2g_tφ/g_φφ while the counter-rotating one has zero coordinate angular velocity, so nothing can counter-rotate or hover there. A stationary observer would need g_tt(u^t)² = -1, impossible once g_tt ≥ 0. The surface g_tt = 0 is the stationary limit, r0 = M + (M² - a² cos²θ)^{1/2}, lying outside r+ except at the poles; the region between them is the ergosphere, part of region I. Example 29.6 gives the equatorial photon potential, whose dependence on σ = sign(L̃) reflects frame dragging, and a light-cone map shows how cones tip in each region.
concepts: Killing vectors and conserved quantities in Kerr
inverse metric of the t-φ block
Kerr equatorial effective potential for massive particles
coordinate angular velocity of tangential light rays
light-cone tilting in the Kerr geometry
key_moves: Express covariant conserved components through contravariant velocities, then invert to find u^t, u^φ.
Set u_φ = 0 and take the ratio u^φ/u^t, which survives only because g^{tφ} ≠ 0.
Solve the quadratic g_tt + 2g_tφ Ω + g_φφ Ω² = 0 for the angular velocity of light.
Specialize to g_tt = 0 to find one root equal to zero and argue from light-cone causality that all bodies must co-rotate.
Give the independent normalization argument against stationary observers.
Solve g_tt = 0 for r to find the stationary limit and compare it with r+ at poles and equator.
Footnote 11 notes g_tt changes sign across the stationary limit, just as it does at r = 2M in Schwarzschild, seeding Section 29.3.

sections.title: Interacting with the Kerr geometry
sections.summary: Describes Penrose's energy-extraction scheme: a particle from infinity enters the ergosphere and splits; one piece crosses the horizon and the other escapes. Local 4-momentum conservation dotted with the timelike-at-infinity Killing vector ξ gives E_out = E_in - E_bh for energies at infinity. Normally E_bh > 0, but inside the ergosphere ξ·ξ = g_tt > 0 so ξ is spacelike and -p_bh·ξ can be negative, allowing E_out > E_in with the hole's mass decreasing. Example 29.7 takes an observer circulating at fixed r and θ with 4-velocity proportional to ξ + Ωη, demands positive locally measured energy for the infalling piece, and obtains E_bh ≥ Ω L_bh; since Ω > 0 in the ergosphere, negative E_bh requires negative L_bh, so the hole also loses angular momentum.
concepts: spacelike Killing vector inside the ergosphere
key_moves: Write p_in = p_out + p_bh at the decay event.
Dot with ξ to turn local conservation into a statement about energies at infinity.
Evaluate ξ·ξ = g_tt and note it is positive inside the ergosphere, so Killing energy need not be positive.
Build a physically allowed observer from Killing vectors, u = u^t(ξ + Ωη), and impose -u·p_bh ≥ 0 for all allowed Ω.
Conclude E_bh ≥ Ω L_bh, hence negative energy implies negative angular momentum for the captured fragment.

sections.title: Chapter summary and the difficulty of deriving Kerr
sections.summary: Four bullet points recap charged holes (unlikely in nature, three regions, repulsive singularity, wormhole travel) and Kerr holes (Boyer-Lindquist form, ring singularity, ergosphere where nothing stays still). One bullet mislabels r0 as an ellipsoidal event horizon; r0 is the stationary limit. A margin essay recounts that Kerr's 1963 announcement gave no derivation, that Kerr and Schild (1965) and Landau and Lifshitz stressed how laborious the calculations are, that Chandrasekhar later presented a better-motivated derivation, and that his perturbation calculations filled hundreds of pages deposited in a Chicago library.
key_moves: Recap the qualitative anatomy of both solutions.
Normalize the fact that the metric was quoted: even experts found it hard to derive.

concepts.name: no-hair theorem
concepts.definition: The result that a stationary black hole in general relativity (with electromagnetism) is completely specified by its mass, electric charge and angular momentum; every other detail of the collapsed matter is radiated away or hidden, so the exterior metric belongs to a three-parameter family.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the observation that a horizon hides the interior, so only globally measurable quantities survive; presented through Wheeler's hair metaphor and used to justify why studying charge and spin covers all black holes.
concepts.notes: The book's justification ('owing to the singularity') is loose; the actual theorems (Israel, Carter, Hawking, Robinson) are uniqueness theorems for stationary vacuum or electrovac black holes.

concepts.name: event horizon
concepts.definition: The boundary of the region from which no future-directed causal curve can reach distant (future null) infinity; for stationary holes it coincides with a null surface where the relevant metric function vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Taken from earlier chapters and used as the reason outside observers cannot learn internal details of the hole.

concepts.name: Reissner-Nordstrom metric
concepts.definition: The static, spherically symmetric solution of the coupled Einstein-Maxwell equations outside a mass M carrying charge q; in geometrized Gaussian units ds² = -f dt² + f⁻¹ dr² + r² dΩ² with f = 1 - 2M/r + q²/r².
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted after arguing that the stress-energy side of the field equation must now include electromagnetic field energy; checked by the q -> 0 Schwarzschild limit.

concepts.name: inner and outer horizons
concepts.definition: The two radii at which the radial metric function of a charged or rotating hole vanishes: r± = M ± (M² - q²)^{1/2} for Reissner-Nordstrom and r± = M ± (M² - a²)^{1/2} for Kerr. The outer one is the event horizon; inside the inner one, surfaces of constant r become timelike again, and in the extended spacetime it acts as a Cauchy horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: Found as coordinate singularities of the quoted metrics; for Kerr they are the zeros of Δ and are displayed as nested surfaces in a cartoon.
concepts.notes: The book calls both 'event horizons'; strictly only r+ is the event horizon. The Cauchy-horizon instability of r- is not discussed.

concepts.name: regions I, II and III of a two-horizon black hole
concepts.definition: The division of a Reissner-Nordstrom or Kerr spacetime into the exterior r > r+ (region I), the between-horizons zone r- < r < r+ (region II) where r is a time-like coordinate and every point lies on a closed trapped surface, and the interior r < r- (region III) where constant-r surfaces are again timelike and the singularity lives.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by cutting spacetime at the two coordinate singularities and checking which regions are static, then labelled on the Penrose diagrams.
concepts.notes: For Kerr the ergosphere belongs to region I, and region III extends to negative r.

concepts.name: closed trapped surface
concepts.definition: A closed spacelike 2-surface such that both the outgoing and ingoing families of orthogonal light rays converge, so its area decreases in every future null direction.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from the Schwarzschild interior to characterize region II of the charged and rotating holes.

concepts.name: timelike singularity
concepts.definition: A curvature singularity whose locus in spacetime is a timelike curve or surface, so it sits beside observers in space rather than lying unavoidably in their future; drawn as a vertical line on a Penrose diagram.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with the spacelike singularities of Schwarzschild and the Big Bang; appears because inside r- the roles of r and t revert to their exterior character.
prerequisites: regions I, II and III of a two-horizon black hole

concepts.name: repulsive singularity
concepts.definition: A singularity that freely falling massive particles never reach, because timelike geodesics turn around before hitting it; in Reissner-Nordstrom the q²/r² term dominates near r = 0 and acts repulsively.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated for the region III singularity of the charged hole, as the reason a traveller can avoid it and continue through the wormhole.
concepts.notes: Holds for geodesics of uncharged particles; accelerated observers or charged particles could reach it.

concepts.name: maximally extended Reissner-Nordstrom Penrose diagram
aliases: Penrose diagram of a charged hole
concepts.definition: The conformal diagram of the analytically extended charged-hole spacetime: an infinite vertical chain in which pairs of asymptotically flat regions I are joined upward through region II to two region-III patches bounded by timelike r = 0 lines, then through another region II to a new pair of region I, and so on.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown in two versions, one with region labels and conformal infinities and one with lines of constant r and t, and used to tell the traveller's story.
prerequisites: regions I, II and III of a two-horizon black hole

concepts.name: passage to another asymptotically flat region
concepts.definition: In the maximally extended charged or rotating black-hole spacetime, a future-directed timelike curve can enter through r+, cross r-, avoid the timelike singularity and exit through another pair of horizons into a different asymptotically flat region; no future-directed curve leads back.
concepts.how_introduced: Told as a traveller's journey on the Penrose tower right after establishing that the singularity is avoidable.
concepts.notes: Relies on the idealized eternal solution; perturbations make the inner horizon singular, so this is not expected physically.

concepts.name: naked singularity
concepts.definition: A curvature singularity not hidden behind any event horizon, as in Reissner-Nordstrom with q² > M² or Kerr with a² > M².
concepts.how_introduced: Only implied: the book notes that for q² > M² the metric has no singular radius except r = 0 and that Kerr horizons exist only for a ≤ M.

concepts.name: extremal black hole
concepts.definition: A black hole whose charge or spin sits at the maximum compatible with a horizon, q² = M² or a = M (J = M²), so the two horizons merge and region II disappears.
concepts.how_introduced: Arises from the square root in r±: for Kerr the maximum angular momentum is read off directly; for Reissner-Nordstrom the vanishing of region II is noted in parentheses.

concepts.name: blueshift at the inner horizon
concepts.definition: An observer crossing the inner horizon of a charged or rotating hole receives light from the whole future history of an exterior region in a finite proper time, so that incoming radiation is blueshifted without bound.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off the Penrose diagram when asking what observers in the charged spacetime would see, paired with the familiar infinite redshift at r+.
concepts.notes: This is the physical seed of the inner-horizon instability, which the book does not mention.

concepts.name: stationary spacetime
concepts.definition: A spacetime admitting a timelike (at infinity) Killing vector, so in adapted coordinates no metric component depends on t; unlike a static spacetime the metric may contain time-space cross terms.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined inside Example 29.1 as the property that the metric components carry no t dependence, in preparation for Kerr.

concepts.name: axisymmetric spacetime
concepts.definition: A spacetime with a spacelike Killing vector whose orbits are closed circles about an axis, so the metric components are independent of the azimuthal angle φ.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the symmetry that survives when rotation breaks spherical symmetry.

concepts.name: general stationary axisymmetric metric
concepts.definition: The line element ds² = -e^{2ν}dt² + e^{2ψ}(dφ - ω dt)² + e^{2μ₂}(dx²)² + e^{2μ₃}(dx³)² with all functions depending only on the two non-symmetry coordinates; ω is an angular velocity that produces the dt dφ cross term.
concepts.how_introduced: Given in Example 29.1 as the most general form compatible with stationarity and axisymmetry, and later matched by rewriting Kerr in eqn 29.6.

concepts.name: off-diagonal metric cross term g_tφ
concepts.definition: A non-zero mixed time-azimuth metric component, which means the coordinate basis vectors e_t and e_φ are not orthogonal; in Kerr g_tφ = -2Mar sin²θ/ρ² and it encodes the rotation of the source.
concepts.how_introduced: Flagged in Example 29.1 as the origin of most new Kerr physics, then shown to cause frame dragging (via g^{tφ}) and the stationary-limit behaviour of light (via g_tφ).

concepts.name: Cotton-Darboux theorem
concepts.definition: The statement that any metric on a three-dimensional manifold can be brought to diagonal form locally by a coordinate change; in four dimensions this is not guaranteed.
concepts.how_introduced: A footnote explaining why the book's earlier metrics could be diagonal, contrasting with the unavoidable cross term in Kerr.

concepts.name: Kerr metric
concepts.definition: The two-parameter (M, a) stationary, axisymmetric, asymptotically flat vacuum solution of the Einstein equation describing a rotating black hole; in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates it has components g_tt = -(1 - 2Mr/ρ²), g_tφ = -2Mar sin²θ/ρ², g_φφ = [(r² + a²)² - a²Δ sin²θ] sin²θ/ρ², g_rr = ρ²/Δ, g_θθ = ρ².
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted after motivating rotation as realistic; checked by reversal symmetry, flat large-r behaviour and the a -> 0 limit; then interrogated by singularities, Killing vectors, test particles and light.
concepts.notes: The book says it is the only exact solution for the exterior of a rotating mass; it is the unique rotating black-hole solution, but the exterior of a rotating star is generally not Kerr.

concepts.name: Boyer-Lindquist coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates (t, r, θ, φ) for Kerr in which t and φ are adapted to the two Killing vectors and r, θ are spheroidal: x = (r² + a²)^{1/2} sinθ cosφ, y = (r² + a²)^{1/2} sinθ sinφ, z = r cosθ, so constant-r surfaces are oblate ellipsoids and r = 0 is a disc of radius a.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as spherical polars with an adjusted radius, with the consequence that the Kerr singularity cannot be a point.
concepts.notes: The printed eqn 29.3 omits the z relation.

concepts.name: Kerr parameter
concepts.definition: The angular momentum per unit mass of the hole, a = J/M, with dimensions of length in geometrized units; a = 0 is Schwarzschild and a = M is extremal.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced alongside the quoted metric as the measure of rotation, with J identified as the angular momentum seen from infinity.

concepts.name: ring singularity
concepts.definition: The curvature singularity of Kerr at ρ² = r² + a² cos²θ = 0, i.e. r = 0 and θ = π/2, which in the Boyer-Lindquist Cartesian picture is a ring x² + y² = a² in the equatorial plane; it is timelike and can be passed through into negative r.
concepts.how_introduced: Found by listing where the metric blows up (ρ = 0 versus Δ = 0) and substituting into the coordinate map.

concepts.name: Kerr horizon area
concepts.definition: The proper area of the outer Kerr horizon on a constant-t slice, A = 8πMr+ = 4π(r+² + a²), which decreases from 16πM² at a = 0 to 8πM² at a = M.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 29.2 restricts the metric to dt = dr = 0 at r = r+, simplifies using r+² + a² = 2Mr+ and integrates the area element.
concepts.notes: Relevant to black-hole thermodynamics (area as entropy) of Chapter 28, which the chapter does not connect explicitly.

concepts.name: Kerr Penrose diagram with negative r
concepts.definition: The conformal diagram of the analytically extended Kerr solution along the symmetry axis: a vertical chain of asymptotically flat regions I, trapped regions II and regions III, where region III continues through the disc r = 0 into a second asymptotically flat region with negative r.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown with lines of constant r; the text explains that because the singularity is a ring, spacetime can be continued past r = 0.

concepts.name: closed timelike curves
concepts.definition: Future-directed timelike curves that return to their starting event; in Kerr they exist near the ring singularity in the negative-r part of region III, where g_φφ < 0 makes circles of constant t, r, θ timelike.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in one sentence while reading the Kerr Penrose diagram.
prerequisites: Kerr Penrose diagram with negative r

concepts.name: Killing vectors and conserved quantities in Kerr
concepts.definition: Because the Kerr metric is independent of t and φ, ξ = ∂_t and η = ∂_φ are Killing vectors and geodesics conserve Ẽ = -ξ·u = -u_t and L̃ = η·u = u_φ; with the cross term these are mixtures u_t = g_tt u^t + g_tφ u^φ and u_φ = g_φt u^t + g_φφ u^φ.
concepts.how_introduced: Carried over from the Schwarzschild recipe, with a warning that the cross terms complicate converting to u^t and u^φ.

concepts.name: inverse metric of the t-φ block
concepts.definition: Inverting the 2x2 matrix of g_tt, g_tφ, g_φφ (determinant -Δ sin²θ for Kerr) to obtain g^{tt}, g^{tφ}, g^{φφ}, which convert conserved covariant components into coordinate velocities.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted in a footnote with the derivation assigned as an exercise; used immediately for frame dragging.

concepts.name: frame dragging
concepts.definition: The effect by which a rotating mass forces nearby freely falling bodies and light to acquire angular velocity in the sense of rotation; a particle with zero conserved angular momentum still has dφ/dt = g^{tφ}/g^{tt} = 2Mar/Σ², which equals the function ω in the stationary-axisymmetric form.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 29.3 drops a particle with u_φ = 0 and shows its coordinate angular velocity is non-zero purely because of the off-diagonal inverse metric.
prerequisites: Killing vectors and conserved quantities in Kerr
inverse metric of the t-φ block
concepts.notes: The book says the particle 'gains' angular momentum; its conserved L̃ stays zero, what appears is angular velocity relative to distant stars.

concepts.name: Kerr equatorial effective potential for massive particles
concepts.definition: For equatorial geodesics, (Ẽ² - 1)/2 = ½(dr/dτ)² + V_eff with V_eff = -M/r + [L̃² - a²(Ẽ² - 1)]/(2r²) - M(L̃ - aẼ)²/r³, which reduces to the Schwarzschild potential at a = 0 and treats co- and counter-rotating orbits differently.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 29.4 finds u^t and u^φ from the conserved quantities, imposes u·u = -1 and solves for u^r, stressing the resemblance to the Schwarzschild case.
prerequisites: Killing vectors and conserved quantities in Kerr

concepts.name: coordinate angular velocity of tangential light rays
concepts.definition: For a photon moving only in t and φ, the null condition g_tt dt² + 2g_tφ dt dφ + g_φφ dφ² = 0 gives two angular velocities Ω± = -g_tφ/g_φφ ± [(g_tφ/g_φφ)² - g_tt/g_φφ]^{1/2}, bracketing the angular velocities any body at that point can have.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 29.5 sets up photons launched in ±φ and solves the quadratic; the special case g_tt = 0 is then examined.

concepts.name: stationary observer
concepts.definition: An observer at fixed r, θ, φ with 4-velocity u^μ = (u^t, 0, 0, 0); normalization requires g_tt (u^t)² = -1, so such observers exist only where g_tt < 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as a second, one-line proof that nothing can remain at rest where g_tt vanishes.

concepts.name: stationary limit surface
concepts.definition: The surface g_tt = 0 (equivalently ρ² = 2Mr), at r0 = M + (M² - a² cos²θ)^{1/2}; inside it no observer can remain at rest relative to infinity. It touches the outer horizon at the poles and reaches r = 2M at the equator.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by noticing that at g_tt = 0 a counter-rotating photon has zero angular velocity, then solving g_tt = 0 for r.
prerequisites: coordinate angular velocity of tangential light rays
concepts.notes: It is not a horizon: signals and particles can escape from inside it. The chapter summary mistakenly calls it an event horizon.

concepts.name: ergosphere
concepts.definition: The region r+ < r < r0 between the outer horizon and the stationary limit, part of the exterior region I, in which every observer must co-rotate with the hole and the Killing vector ∂_t is spacelike, permitting negative Killing energy.
concepts.how_introduced: Named once the stationary limit is found; drawn in side and top views for a near-extremal hole and in a 3D cartoon; exploited in Section 29.3.

concepts.name: Kerr photon effective potential
concepts.definition: For equatorial photons, (1/L̃²)(dr/dλ)² = 1/b² - W_eff with W_eff = (1/r²)[1 - (a/b)² - (2M/r)(1 - σa/b)²], where b = L̃/Ẽ in magnitude and σ = sign(L̃) distinguishes prograde from retrograde light.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 29.6 quotes it (derivation left as an exercise) and interprets the σ dependence as frame dragging.

concepts.name: prograde and retrograde motion
concepts.definition: Orbits or rays whose angular momentum is aligned (prograde) or anti-aligned (retrograde) with the hole's spin; in Kerr their potentials, orbital radii and allowed angular velocities differ.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears through the (L̃ - aẼ) and σ factors in the effective potentials and the two roots of the tangential null condition.
prerequisites: Kerr equatorial effective potential for massive particles

concepts.name: light-cone tilting in the Kerr geometry
concepts.definition: The progressive tipping of local future light cones: far away they are upright, at the stationary limit they touch the direction of rest, inside the ergosphere they point entirely in the rotation direction, between the horizons they point entirely inward, and inside r- outward motion becomes possible again.
concepts.how_introduced: Summarized by a top-down diagram of small cone sections drawn across the regions.
prerequisites: regions I, II and III of a two-horizon black hole

concepts.name: Penrose process
aliases: energy extraction from a rotating black hole
concepts.definition: A mechanism in which a body entering the ergosphere splits into two, one fragment falling through the horizon on a negative-Killing-energy trajectory and the other escaping with more energy at infinity than the original body had, the excess being taken from the hole's mass and spin.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as Penrose's suggestion and justified by local momentum conservation, a dot product with ξ, and the spacelike character of ξ in the ergosphere.
concepts.notes: The maximum extractable energy (down to the irreducible mass) and the link with the area theorem are not discussed.

concepts.name: Killing energy and negative-energy orbits
concepts.definition: The conserved quantity E = -ξ·p built from the stationary Killing vector; it equals energy measured by an observer at rest at infinity, but where ξ is spacelike it is not a locally measured energy and can take negative values on physically allowed trajectories.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from the Hawking radiation chapter and used to convert the decay's momentum balance into energies at infinity.

concepts.name: spacelike Killing vector inside the ergosphere
concepts.definition: The norm of the stationary Killing vector is ξ·ξ = g_tt, which is negative outside the stationary limit and positive inside, so ξ becomes spacelike in the ergosphere, just as ∂_t does inside r = 2M in Schwarzschild.
concepts.how_introduced: Planted in footnote 11 and cashed in when explaining why Killing energy is no longer bounded below.

concepts.name: positivity of locally measured energy
concepts.definition: Any physical observer with 4-velocity u measures a particle energy E = -u·p that is non-negative for future-directed timelike or null momentum.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from the Hawking radiation argument and imposed for a circulating observer in Example 29.7.

concepts.name: circularly rotating observer
aliases: observer at fixed r and θ
concepts.definition: An observer who keeps r and θ fixed but circulates with angular velocity Ω = dφ/dt, so u = u^t(ξ + Ωη); inside the ergosphere Ω must be positive (co-rotating).
concepts.how_introduced: Constructed in Example 29.7 from the two Killing vectors to obtain an energy bound valid everywhere in the ergosphere.
prerequisites: Killing vectors and conserved quantities in Kerr

concepts.name: spin-down by energy extraction
concepts.definition: Because locally positive energy requires E_bh ≥ Ω L_bh with Ω > 0 in the ergosphere, a fragment with negative Killing energy must carry negative angular momentum, so the Penrose process lowers both the mass and angular momentum of the hole.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in Example 29.7 and stated as the conclusion of the chapter's application.

concepts.name: conservation of 4-momentum in decays
concepts.definition: At a local event where one particle splits into two, the 4-momenta satisfy p_in = p_out + p_bh, whatever the curvature of spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the starting point for the Penrose process.

concepts.name: Kerr-Newman metric
concepts.definition: The stationary black-hole solution carrying mass, charge and angular momentum simultaneously, which contains both Reissner-Nordstrom and Kerr as special cases.
concepts.how_introduced: Named only in a biographical footnote on Kerr.

concepts.name: asymptotic flatness
concepts.definition: The property that the metric approaches Minkowski form at large distances, so that mass and angular momentum can be measured from infinity and the Penrose diagram has i0, i± and null infinities.
concepts.how_introduced: Checked for Kerr by taking r large, and used to label region I in the Penrose diagrams.

key_equations.name: Reissner-Nordstrom line element
key_equations.meaning: Geometry outside a spherically symmetric charged mass; the q² term is the gravitational effect of the electric field's energy. Reduces to Schwarzschild when q = 0.
key_equations.symbols: M mass, q charge (both lengths in geometrized Gaussian units), (t, r, θ, φ) Schwarzschild-like coordinates

key_equations.name: Reissner-Nordstrom horizon radii
key_equations.meaning: Zeros of the metric function; for q² < M² two horizons, for q² = M² one degenerate horizon, for q² > M² none (naked singularity).
key_equations.symbols: r+ outer horizon, r- inner horizon

key_equations.name: General stationary axisymmetric line element
key_equations.meaning: Most general metric with time-translation and rotational symmetry; expanding the second term yields a dt dφ cross term proportional to ω.
key_equations.symbols: ν, ψ, ω, μ₂, μ₃ functions of x², x³ only; ω is an angular velocity

key_equations.name: Boyer-Lindquist to Cartesian map
key_equations.meaning: Spheroidal coordinates: constant-r surfaces are oblate ellipsoids and r = 0 is a disc of radius a. The z relation is missing from the printed equation and has been restored here.

key_equations.name: Kerr line element in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Exterior and interior geometry of a rotating black hole; the dt dφ term carries the rotation.
key_equations.symbols: Δ = r² - 2Mr + a², ρ² = r² + a² cos²θ, a = J/M

key_equations.name: Kerr auxiliary functions
key_equations.meaning: Δ vanishes at the horizons, ρ vanishes on the ring singularity; a is angular momentum per unit mass.
key_equations.symbols: J angular momentum measured at infinity

key_equations.name: Kerr metric components
key_equations.meaning: Component list used throughout the examples; negative g_tφ for a > 0 means rotation in the +φ sense.

key_equations.name: Kerr Killing vectors and conserved quantities
key_equations.meaning: t- and φ-independence give two Killing vectors and hence conserved energy and angular momentum per unit mass along geodesics.
key_equations.symbols: ξ stationary Killing vector, η axial Killing vector, u 4-velocity

key_equations.name: Kerr metric in ω form
key_equations.meaning: Shows Kerr is an instance of eqn 29.2, with ω the frame-dragging angular velocity. The book prints the dr² coefficient as ρ²/Δ²; the correct coefficient, consistent with eqn 29.4, is ρ²/Δ.
key_equations.symbols: Σ² book's notation for (r² + a²)² - a²Δ sin²θ (called A or Σ in other texts)

key_equations.name: Kerr horizon radii
key_equations.meaning: Where Δ = 0; horizons exist only for a ≤ M, giving the maximum spin J = M². At a = 0, r+ = 2M and r- = 0.

key_equations.name: Ring singularity location
key_equations.meaning: The physical curvature singularity of Kerr is a ring of coordinate radius a in the equatorial plane.

key_equations.name: Induced metric on the outer horizon
key_equations.meaning: Setting dt = dr = 0 at r = r+ and using r+² + a² = 2Mr+ gives the 2-geometry of the horizon, which is not a round sphere.

key_equations.name: Kerr horizon area
key_equations.meaning: Area of the event horizon; 16πM² for Schwarzschild, 8πM² for extremal Kerr. The book writes the integrand as g, the determinant; it should be the square root of the determinant of the induced 2-metric.

key_equations.name: Conserved quantities with cross terms
key_equations.meaning: Each conserved quantity mixes time and azimuthal velocity components because the metric is not diagonal.

key_equations.name: Coordinate angular velocity as a ratio
key_equations.meaning: Angular velocity seen from infinity equals the ratio of contravariant velocity components.

key_equations.name: Inverse Kerr metric (t-φ block)
key_equations.meaning: Needed to raise indices on the conserved components; obtained by inverting the 2x2 block whose determinant is -Δ sin²θ.

key_equations.name: Ratio of inverse metric components
key_equations.meaning: The frame-dragging angular velocity; it is identical to ω = 2Mar/Σ² in eqn 29.6, a connection the text leaves implicit.

key_equations.name: Raising indices on the 4-velocity
key_equations.meaning: Converts conserved covariant components into coordinate velocities.

key_equations.name: Frame dragging of a zero-angular-momentum particle
key_equations.meaning: A body with no conserved angular momentum still circulates in the sense of the hole's rotation.

key_equations.name: Equatorial contravariant velocities
key_equations.meaning: Time and azimuthal velocity components for θ = π/2 geodesics in terms of conserved Ẽ and L̃.

key_equations.name: Radial energy equation
key_equations.meaning: Same structure as the Schwarzschild energy equation: a kinetic term plus an effective potential.

key_equations.name: Kerr equatorial effective potential
key_equations.meaning: Spin modifies the centrifugal term and the relativistic 1/r³ term; the (L̃ - aẼ) combination makes prograde and retrograde orbits differ. At a = 0 it becomes the Schwarzschild potential.

key_equations.name: Null condition for tangential photons
key_equations.meaning: Light moving purely in φ at fixed r, θ.

key_equations.name: Angular velocities of light
key_equations.meaning: The two roots bound the angular velocity of any body at that location.

key_equations.name: Light angular velocities where g_tt = 0
key_equations.meaning: On the stationary limit the co-rotating ray moves while the counter-rotating ray has zero coordinate angular velocity; nothing can move against the rotation.

key_equations.name: Condition for a stationary observer
key_equations.meaning: Hovering is possible only where g_tt < 0; fails at and inside the stationary limit.

key_equations.name: Where g_tt vanishes
key_equations.meaning: Footnote condition defining the stationary limit surface.

key_equations.name: Stationary limit surface
key_equations.meaning: Outer boundary of the ergosphere: equals r+ at the poles and 2M at the equator.
key_equations.symbols: θ polar angle from the rotation axis

key_equations.name: Photon radial equation in Kerr
key_equations.meaning: Equatorial photon motion governed by an impact parameter and an orientation-dependent potential.
key_equations.symbols: λ affine parameter, b impact parameter (magnitude of L̃/Ẽ), σ = sign(L̃)

key_equations.name: Kerr photon effective potential
key_equations.meaning: The σ dependence makes prograde and retrograde light see different barriers; reduces to the Schwarzschild W_eff at a = 0.

key_equations.name: Momentum conservation at the split
key_equations.meaning: Local 4-momentum balance when the infalling body divides in the ergosphere.

key_equations.name: Energy balance at infinity
key_equations.meaning: Dotting 29.25 with ξ gives conserved Killing energies; extraction occurs if the captured piece has negative Killing energy.

key_equations.name: Norm of the stationary Killing vector
key_equations.meaning: ξ is spacelike in the ergosphere, so -p·ξ is no longer forced to be positive.

key_equations.name: 4-velocity of a circulating observer
key_equations.meaning: Observer at fixed r and θ rotating with angular velocity Ω.

key_equations.name: Observer velocity from Killing vectors
key_equations.meaning: Writing the observer in terms of symmetry generators so that dot products with p become conserved quantities.

key_equations.name: Positive local energy of the infalling fragment
key_equations.meaning: Holds for every Ω that makes u timelike (u·u = -1 achievable).

key_equations.name: Energy-angular momentum bound
key_equations.meaning: With Ω > 0 in the ergosphere, E_bh < 0 forces L_bh < 0: extraction spins the hole down.

key_equations.name: Alternative form of g_tt (exercise)
key_equations.meaning: Identity used to see where g_tt changes sign.

key_equations.name: Alternative form of g_φφ (exercise)
key_equations.meaning: Form of g_φφ that makes the horizon simplification in 29.8 immediate.

key_equations.name: Horizon 2-metric (exercise restatement of 29.8)
key_equations.meaning: Exercise version; the printed first term reads ρ+ dθ² and should be ρ+² dθ².

key_equations.name: Horizon area (exercise restatement of 29.9)
key_equations.meaning: Same area integral; the printed integrand again shows g where the square root of the 2D determinant is meant.

key_equations.name: The t-φ metric block to invert (exercise)
key_equations.meaning: Inverting this block reproduces eqn 29.12; the determinant value is given in the book's answers appendix.

figures.label: Fig. 29.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Conformal diagram of the maximally extended charged black hole, with line styles distinguishing the outer horizon, inner horizon and the r = 0 singularity.
figures.visual_description: A tall, narrow vertical tower built from two stacked copies of one pattern. In each copy a pair of region-I diamonds sits at the far left and right; each has null edges labelled future and past null infinity, a spatial-infinity vertex i0 at its outer corner, and filled dots at its top (i+) and bottom (i-) corners. Between the two I diamonds lies a region-II diamond above and another below. Faint dotted diagonals labelled r = r+ cross through the centre between the I pair, and dashed diagonals labelled r = r- form an X below each lower II, leaving a region-III triangle on each side. Each III is closed on its outer side by a vertical double line labelled r = 0 that joins the i- dot of the I diamond above to the i+ dot of the I diamond below. Double r = 0 lines ending in dots also rise off the top of the drawing and descend off the bottom, signalling that the chain continues without end. The line styles agree with the caption: dotted for r+, dashed for r-, doubled for r = 0.
figures.what_it_teaches: The charged hole's global causal structure: an infinite sequence of universes linked by trapped regions and inner regions whose singularities are vertical, i.e. timelike, lines that a traveller can steer around.
concepts: regions I, II and III of a two-horizon black hole
passage to another asymptotically flat region

redesign.idea: Explorable Reissner-Nordstrom tower where the learner draws a worldline with a stylus, and the app enforces the 45-degree light-cone rule, flags when the curve hits r = 0, and highlights each region crossed; a q/M slider morphs the diagram from Schwarzschild (q = 0) to the extremal case (region II collapses).
redesign.interaction: Drag to sketch a timelike path; slider for q/M; toggle to show which directions are allowed at the cursor; button to animate a one-way trip into the next universe with a counter of universes visited.

figures.label: Fig. 29.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: The charged-hole Penrose diagram again, now filled with families of constant-r and constant-t surfaces.
figures.visual_description: A fragment of the charged-hole tower, offset like a staircase. At upper left a region-I diamond, bounded by future and past null infinity, is packed with bold solid lens-shaped curves that all run from its top dot (i+) down to its bottom dot (i-): the timelike surfaces of constant r. Short tick marks cut across these curves; they stand in for the spacelike surfaces of constant t, which the caption calls dashed. Down and to the right, the region-II diamond has solid curves stretched sideways between its left and right dots (constant r is now spacelike), again crossed by ticks. At lower left, a region-III wedge beside a vertical double line labelled r = 0 holds solid curves that run from top to bottom alongside the singularity. The right-hand region I and the upper region II, whose top closes in a dashed X between two further double r = 0 lines, contain no grid. A faint dotted diagonal is labelled r = r+ and a dashed diagonal r = r-.
figures.what_it_teaches: How the causal character of constant-r surfaces alternates timelike, spacelike, timelike from region I to II to III, which is why r = 0 is timelike and why region II forces motion toward smaller r.
concepts: regions I, II and III of a two-horizon black hole

redesign.idea: Coordinate-grid overlay on the Reissner-Nordstrom Penrose diagram: hovering any point shows the local light cone, the constant-r and constant-t curves through it, and a label stating whether r is timelike or spacelike there.
redesign.interaction: Hover or tap a point; sliders for the r value of a highlighted curve (watch it jump from region I to II to III as r crosses r+ and r-); toggle to animate a constant-r observer's world line.

figures.label: Fig. 29.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Cartoon of the nested special surfaces of a Kerr black hole.
figures.visual_description: A hand-drawn 3D cutaway. A vertical line is the rotation axis, with a small circular arrow at the top labelled 'Rotation axis'. A very wide, flattened ellipsoid labelled 'Static limit' encloses everything; the gap between it and a sphere inside is marked I and, via an arrow, 'Ergosphere'. The sphere, labelled 'Outer event Horizon r+', encloses region II; inside it a smaller cap-like surface labelled 'Inner event Horizon r-' encloses region III. At the centre, in the equatorial plane marked by dashed lines, a small bold ring is labelled 'Physical ring singularity'. The static-limit ellipsoid meets the horizon on the axis at the top.
figures.what_it_teaches: The geography of Kerr from outside in: stationary limit, ergosphere (still outside the horizon), outer horizon, inner horizon, and the ring singularity, with the ergosphere touching the horizon at the poles.
concepts: regions I, II and III of a two-horizon black hole

redesign.idea: 3D Kerr anatomy viewer with surfaces computed from the formulas r0(θ), r+, r- and the ring, embedded with the Boyer-Lindquist Cartesian map so shapes are honest rather than cartoon.
redesign.interaction: Orbit camera; spin slider a/M from 0 to 1 (ergosphere grows from nothing, horizons approach each other and merge at a = M); clip-plane slider to cut open the surfaces; click a surface for its equation and physical meaning.

figures.label: Fig. 29.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram for maximally extended Kerr, with constant-r curves and the r = 0 locus in region III.
figures.visual_description: A vertical stack of diamonds in three columns. The left and right columns alternate a region I (with future and past null infinity labels on its outer edges) and a region III; the central column holds region-II diamonds between them. Families of dashed constant-r curves bow top-to-bottom inside regions I and III and side-to-side inside region II. Faint dotted diagonals are labelled r = r+; the r = r- diagonals look dashed in this reproduction, though the caption calls them dot-dashed. Each region-III diamond contains one solid curve joining its bottom and top vertices, marking r = 0. The outer edges of the III diamonds are solid null lines, the infinity of the negative-r region beyond the ring. Unlike the Reissner-Nordstrom figures there is no double singularity line.
figures.what_it_teaches: Unlike Reissner-Nordstrom, Kerr's r = 0 is not an edge: the ring can be bypassed or passed through into a negative-r region, and the same traveller story of I -> II -> III -> II -> I applies.
concepts: Kerr Penrose diagram with negative r
passage to another asymptotically flat region

redesign.idea: Side-by-side comparison of the Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordstrom and Kerr Penrose diagrams sharing one timeline, with a slider that morphs between them and highlights where the singularity sits and whether it is spacelike, timelike or a passable locus.
redesign.interaction: Choose black-hole type; drag a traveller along a worldline; toggle constant-r curves; click region III to open an inset explaining negative r and where closed timelike curves appear.

figures.label: Fig. 29.5(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Side view of the ergosphere of an almost extremal Kerr hole.
figures.visual_description: A vertical rotation axis with a curling arrow at the top. A white central disc (the horizon, radius indicated by an arrow labelled r+) is surrounded by a grey region whose outer boundary looks like two overlapping circles bulging out on the left and right and pinching in to meet the white disc at the top and bottom where the axis crosses. A second arrow from the centre, at angle θ from the axis, reaches the outer grey boundary.
figures.what_it_teaches: The stationary limit r0(θ) coincides with the horizon on the rotation axis and is farthest out at the equator, so the ergosphere is a pumpkin-shaped shell that is thickest in the equatorial plane.

redesign.idea: Polar plot of r0(θ) and r+ in the meridian plane that the learner can reshape with the spin parameter, with a probe at angle θ reporting r0 - r+ and whether a hovering observer is allowed there.
redesign.interaction: Spin slider a/M; draggable probe on the θ arc; readout of g_tt sign at the probe; toggle between plotting Boyer-Lindquist r directly and the Cartesian spheroidal embedding.

figures.label: Fig. 29.5(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Top-down view of the same near-extremal ergosphere.
figures.visual_description: A white inner disc (horizon) containing a curved arrow indicating counter-clockwise rotation, surrounded by a uniform grey annulus (ergosphere) with a circular outer edge; panel label (b).
figures.what_it_teaches: Seen from above the pole, the ergosphere is a ring-shaped zone around the horizon in the equatorial plane where rotation dominates.

redesign.idea: Equatorial-plane view in which small test particles and hovering rockets are released; outside the grey ring rockets can hold still, inside it every marker is swept around in the rotation direction regardless of thrust.
redesign.interaction: Click to place a rocket and set its thrust direction; spin slider; play button to watch trajectories and a readout of the minimum allowed angular velocity at each radius.

figures.label: Fig. 29.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Map of how light cones are oriented across the regions of the Kerr geometry.
figures.visual_description: A top-down equatorial view. A large grey annulus labelled 'ergosphere' has its outer edge marked 'stationary limit surface'; its inner edge is the circle r = r+, and a smaller circle inside is r = r-. At the centre a small fuzzy-edged circle is labelled 'singularity'. Small open circles with a black dot mark local light-cone cross-sections: far outside, the dot sits at the centre of its circle; on the stationary limit the dot lies on the circle's edge; inside the ergosphere and between the horizons the circles are displaced, drawn as tear-drop shapes whose dot lies outside the circle, pointing around and inward; inside r- the tear-drops point in varied directions near the singularity.
figures.what_it_teaches: Motion possibilities at each radius: unconstrained far away, forced co-rotation in the ergosphere, forced infall between the horizons, and renewed freedom (including moving away from the singularity) inside the inner horizon.
concepts: light-cone tilting in the Kerr geometry

redesign.idea: Light-cone field computed from the Kerr metric on the equatorial plane: each grid point shows the allowed range of (dr/dt, dφ/dt) as a wedge, so learners see the wedge exclude 'stay still' at r0 and exclude 'outward' at r+.
redesign.interaction: Spin slider; radial probe that displays the two tangential light angular velocities from eqn 29.20 and the radial null speeds; toggle between coordinate and locally non-rotating frames.

worked_examples.label: Example 29.1
worked_examples.problem: What is the most general line element for a spacetime that is both stationary and axisymmetric?
worked_examples.method: Impose independence of t and φ, let the remaining functions depend on the other two coordinates, and allow an angular-velocity function ω to couple dφ and dt.
worked_examples.key_insight: Rotation introduces a non-removable dt dφ cross term, unlike every metric used earlier in the book, and this term will be responsible for Kerr's novel effects.
worked_examples.result: ds² = -e^{2ν}dt² + e^{2ψ}(dφ - ω dt)² + e^{2μ₂}(dx²)² + e^{2μ₃}(dx³)², with a cross term ∝ ω dφ dt.

worked_examples.label: Example 29.2
worked_examples.problem: Find the area of the outer horizon of a Kerr black hole.
worked_examples.method: Set dt = dr = 0 and r = r+ in the metric, use r+² + a² = 2Mr+ to collapse g_φφ to (2Mr+/ρ+)² sin²θ, then integrate the square root of the 2D metric determinant over θ and φ.
worked_examples.key_insight: The horizon is a surface of constant t and r whose 2-geometry is not a round sphere, yet its area has a compact closed form.
worked_examples.result: A = 8πMr+ (the printed integrand omits the square root).

worked_examples.label: Example 29.3
worked_examples.problem: A particle is released with zero angular momentum (u_φ = 0). Does it fall straight in?
worked_examples.method: Write dφ/dt = u^φ/u^t, raise indices with the inverse metric so that u^φ = g^{φt} u_t and u^t = g^{tt} u_t, and take the ratio.
worked_examples.key_insight: Zero conserved angular momentum does not mean zero angular velocity: the off-diagonal inverse metric component forces circulation.
worked_examples.result: dφ/dt = g^{φt}/g^{tt} = 2Mra/[(r² + a²)² - a²Δ sin²θ] ≠ 0 (frame dragging).
concepts: inverse metric of the t-φ block
Killing vectors and conserved quantities in Kerr

worked_examples.label: Example 29.4
worked_examples.problem: Obtain the effective-potential description of equatorial massive-particle motion in Kerr.
worked_examples.method: Invert the conserved-quantity relations at θ = π/2 for u^t and u^φ, set u^θ = 0, impose u·u = -1 and solve for (dr/dτ)²; details are an exercise.
worked_examples.key_insight: The Schwarzschild energy-equation format survives, but spin enters through a²(Ẽ² - 1) in the centrifugal term and through (L̃ - aẼ)² in the strong-field term.
worked_examples.result: (Ẽ² - 1)/2 = ½(dr/dτ)² + V_eff, with V_eff = -M/r + [L̃² - a²(Ẽ² - 1)]/(2r²) - M(L̃ - aẼ)²/r³.
concepts: Kerr equatorial effective potential for massive particles

worked_examples.label: Example 29.5
worked_examples.problem: How fast, in angle, can light travelling tangentially (±φ) move at a given point of the equatorial Kerr geometry?
worked_examples.method: Impose the null condition with only dt and dφ non-zero and solve the resulting quadratic for dφ/dt.
worked_examples.key_insight: The two roots are not symmetric about zero; the offset -g_tφ/g_φφ is a dragging angular velocity, and when g_tt = 0 the retrograde root is exactly zero.
worked_examples.result: dφ/dt = -g_tφ/g_φφ ± [(g_tφ/g_φφ)² - g_tt/g_φφ]^{1/2}; for g_tt = 0, dφ/dt = -2g_tφ/g_φφ or 0.
concepts: coordinate angular velocity of tangential light rays

worked_examples.problem: Embedded calculation after Example 29.5: can any observer remain at rest where g_tt = 0, and where is that surface?
worked_examples.method: Argue first from light cones (if counter-rotating light cannot move backward, no body can) and then from normalization of a static 4-velocity; solve g_tt = 0, i.e. r² - 2Mr + a² cos²θ = 0, for the larger root.
worked_examples.key_insight: Being unable to stay still is a different condition from being unable to escape; the first happens at r0, outside the horizon r+.
worked_examples.result: Stationary limit r0 = M + (M² - a² cos²θ)^{1/2}; ergosphere r+ ≤ r ≤ r0.

worked_examples.label: Example 29.6
worked_examples.problem: State the effective-potential description of equatorial photon orbits in Kerr.
worked_examples.method: Quote the radial equation in terms of the impact parameter b and a potential W_eff, with derivation deferred to an exercise.
worked_examples.key_insight: The photon potential depends on σ = sign(L̃), so prograde and retrograde light face different barriers, a direct signature of frame dragging.

worked_examples.problem: Embedded calculation opening Section 29.3: how can splitting a particle in the ergosphere yield net energy at infinity?
worked_examples.method: Write local 4-momentum conservation, dot with ξ to express energies at infinity, then evaluate ξ·ξ = g_tt and note it is positive inside the ergosphere.
worked_examples.key_insight: Conservation of Killing energy is never violated; what changes is that a spacelike ξ lets a physically allowed fragment carry negative Killing energy into the hole.
worked_examples.result: E_out^∞ = E_in^∞ - E_bh^∞ > E_in^∞ whenever E_bh^∞ < 0, which is possible only where ξ is spacelike.
concepts: spacelike Killing vector inside the ergosphere

worked_examples.label: Example 29.7
worked_examples.problem: Show that a negative-energy fragment captured in the Penrose process must also reduce the hole's angular momentum.
worked_examples.method: Use an observer at fixed r, θ circulating with angular velocity Ω, write u = u^t(ξ + Ωη), require that observer to measure non-negative energy for the fragment, and translate the dot products into E and L.
worked_examples.key_insight: Constructing observers from Killing vectors turns a local positivity statement into an inequality between conserved quantities.
worked_examples.result: E_bh ≥ Ω L_bh with Ω > 0 in the ergosphere, so E_bh < 0 requires L_bh < 0 and the hole spins down.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Hair as a metaphor for every detail of a collapsed object beyond mass, charge and spin
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Wheeler's slogan that black holes are bald compresses a uniqueness theorem into an image: all distinguishing features are shed.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The slogan refers to stationary end states; during formation and ringdown the hole does have 'hair' (multipole moments) that decays away, and in theories with extra fields hair can exist.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Collapse animation where a lumpy, magnetized, spinning star sheds its features as gravitational and electromagnetic waves until only three sliders (M, q, J) remain.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Boyer-Lindquist coordinates as ordinary spherical polars with a stretched radius
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Replacing r by (r² + a²)^{1/2} in the x and y relations turns spheres into oblate ellipsoids and r = 0 into a disc.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only a picture of the coordinate labels in a fictitious flat space; the physical geometry of Kerr is curved and the surfaces' intrinsic shapes differ.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Morphing grid: slide a from 0 upward and watch the constant-r spheres flatten into ellipsoids and the origin open into a disc.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Reversing the film of a spinning object reverses its spin
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why the metric is unchanged under t -> -t together with φ -> -φ, but not under either alone.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A symmetry check only; does not illuminate dynamics.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Travelling through a one-way tunnel into a new universe
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: passage to another asymptotically flat region
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The Penrose tower is narrated as a traveller's itinerary, making abstract causal structure into a journey with irreversible steps.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The eternal maximally extended solution is not what forms in realistic collapse, and inner-horizon instability likely seals the tunnel.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Choose-your-path game on the Penrose tower where each move must stay inside the light cone and the goal is to reach a new region I.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The ergosphere behaves toward standing still the way the Schwarzschild interior behaves toward staying at fixed r
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: spacelike Killing vector inside the ergosphere
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Footnote 11 points out that g_tt flips sign across the stationary limit exactly as it does at r = 2M, so arguments that used the sign flip (Hawking radiation) transfer to the ergosphere.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: At r = 2M the flip coincides with the horizon; in Kerr the flip happens outside the horizon, so escape remains possible.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split-screen: Schwarzschild on the left and Kerr on the right, shading where ∂_t is timelike or spacelike as the learner moves a probe inward.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Light rays as a universal speed limit that fences in all motion
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: coordinate angular velocity of tangential light rays
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: If even a photon aimed backward cannot make retrograde progress, no massive body can, however much angular momentum it has.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Coordinate angular velocity is a statement about the view from infinity; locally every observer still measures light at speed 1.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Two photons launched in opposite directions from a probe point; as the probe moves inward the backward photon's progress slows and stops at r0.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Swimming in a whirlpool or walking against a fast moving walkway (tutor-suggested, not in the book)
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives novices a bodily sense of why, inside the ergosphere, no effort keeps you stationary relative to the distant shore.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Suggests a medium flowing through space; in GR it is the local light-cone structure itself that tilts, and nothing exerts a drag force.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: River-model animation where space is shown flowing and rotating, with a warning overlay that the flow is a coordinate picture.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Charged black holes are an important class of astrophysical objects.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Any appreciable charge would attract opposite charges from surrounding plasma and be neutralized; Reissner-Nordstrom is studied for its structure, not realism.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is the next exact solution after Schwarzschild and appears prominently in textbooks.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: An electron is a tiny Reissner-Nordstrom black hole, since it is point-like and charged.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The book notes the description ignores spin; moreover an electron's charge and spin vastly exceed its mass in geometrized units (q/M ~ 10^21, a/M ~ 10^44 by our estimate), so even Kerr-Newman would have no horizon, and quantum effects dominate.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: A point charge seems like the ideal infinitely dense charged object.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Every black-hole singularity lies unavoidably in the future of anyone who crosses the horizon, as in Schwarzschild.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Inside the inner horizon of charged and rotating holes the singularity is timelike, so timelike curves can avoid it; for Reissner-Nordstrom free fall never reaches it.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Schwarzschild is the only interior most learners have studied.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A Kerr black hole has a point singularity at r = 0 like Schwarzschild.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In Boyer-Lindquist coordinates r = 0 is a disc; the curvature singularity is its rim, a ring of radius a in the equatorial plane, and the disc interior can be crossed to negative r.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The symbol r suggests radial distance and r = 0 suggests a point.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A particle dropped with zero angular momentum falls radially without rotating.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Its conserved L̃ stays zero but its angular velocity dφ/dt is non-zero because of the off-diagonal inverse metric; it circulates with the hole.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Newtonian gravity and in Schwarzschild, zero angular momentum means purely radial motion.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: With a powerful enough rocket, an observer could hover at any point outside the event horizon.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Inside the stationary limit the future light cone excludes the world line of rest; no thrust permits a stationary observer there, even though escape outward is still possible.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Schwarzschild the static limit and the horizon coincide at r = 2M, so 'outside the horizon' and 'can hover' feel equivalent.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The ergosphere is part of the black hole's interior, so anything entering it is lost.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The ergosphere lies outside r+ and belongs to region I; particles and light can leave it, which is exactly what makes the Penrose process possible.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Its cartoon sits snugly around the horizon, and the chapter summary itself mislabels its boundary as an event horizon.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Penrose process creates energy from nothing or violates conservation of energy.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Local 4-momentum and total Killing energy are conserved; the extra energy comes from the hole, whose mass and angular momentum decrease when it swallows a negative-energy, negative-angular-momentum fragment.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The escaping fragment has more energy than the incoming particle, which looks like a free lunch.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Negative Killing energy means a particle has negative energy in its own or any observer's frame.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Every physical observer still measures positive energy; only the Killing quantity -ξ·p can be negative, because ξ is spacelike in the ergosphere and is not an observer's 4-velocity there.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The same letter E is used for Killing energy and measured energy.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Kerr metric describes the exterior of any rotating star or planet, just as Schwarzschild describes any spherical one.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: There is no Birkhoff theorem for rotation; a rotating star's exterior has multipole moments that generally differ from Kerr's. Kerr is the unique end state for a rotating black hole.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The text calls Kerr the only known exact solution for the region outside a rotating mass.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The surface r0 is the event horizon of a Kerr black hole.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: r0 is the stationary limit where g_tt vanishes; the event horizon is at r+, where Δ vanishes, and the two coincide only on the rotation axis.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both are places where a Schwarzschild-trained intuition expects the horizon, and the chapter summary uses this wording.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A traveller could really use a charged or rotating black hole to reach another universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The multi-universe tower belongs to the idealized eternal solution; realistic collapse does not produce the past regions, and radiation blueshifted at the inner horizon is expected to turn it into a singularity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The book presents the trip enthusiastically as a consequence of the geometry.
